title: The warm-up that counts
summary: Start every sitting with five minutes of scales and arpeggios, the map of the keyboard in your fingers.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A keyboard spanning two octaves from middle C. C4 up to C5, all seven white notes plus the octave, are highlighted as an example one-octave C major scale, since the exact scale is the one your own teacher has set.

steps.title: The warm-up that counts
steps.body:
A scale is not a chore before the real practice. It is a map of the keyboard: which fingers cross under, which black keys sit where, how the hand moves without looking. Practise the map and the piece gets a little easier, because the hand already knows the shape.

From this week, five minutes of scales and arpeggios open every sitting, before the piece.

1. Play the scale your teacher has set, both hands together, slowly, four times.
2. Play the matching arpeggio four times, using the same hand shape as the scale.
3. Say the fingering out loud once on the way up, if a spot still trips you.
4. Move on to the piece.

Keep this five-minute warm-up at the start of every sitting from now on, every week, not only this one. A pianist plays the same handful of scales for years, because the map keeps paying off long after it stops feeling new.

figure.alt: The same example scale, C4 up to C5, highlighted on a two-octave keyboard: the five minutes of scale and arpeggio that now open every sitting, before the piece.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: five minutes of scale and arpeggio, then the piece's hard bars
Sitting 2: the warm-up, then the piece once through
Sitting 3: the warm-up, then the piece once through
Sitting 4: the warm-up, then the piece once through as if recording
An old piece played once, warm-up first

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Play the warm-up once, say its name, then play this week's piece once through, hands in the frame.

extras.title: A scale of your own
extras.body:
Make up a five-note scale that is not one you already know.

Start with a question: what if a scale skipped a note that a normal scale always keeps?

Three constraints: use only the white keys, keep one steady beat, and start and end on the same note.

Sketch first: write the note names on paper before you play them.

You know it works when you can play it up and down twice without stopping to think.
